script.opening: "Doctor, it’s Frank Tully — Joan’s husband. I’ll not waste your time: I need something to make her sleep. A proper tablet. She’s up at two, three in the morning, dressed, rattling the front door wanting her mother — her mother died in 1987, doctor. I steer her back and she cries and fights me and then at breakfast she’s my Joan again and remembers none of it. I can’t… (long pause) I’m eighty-three. I can’t keep doing nights."

facts.text: Six weeks, most nights, 2–3am: dresses, door, "going to see Mother", tearful resistance when redirected, settles after 1–2 hours of Frank’s patient talking. Worse since the clocks changed and since Joan’s knees "have been giving her gyp".

If asked: Joan naps 11–1 and again after tea ("it’s the only peace I get, I let her sleep"). Tea and biscuits through the afternoon. TV until 10. Curtains thin — streetlight floods the room. She walks less than she did — the knees.

Grimaces on standing, rubs them at night, paracetamol "now and then, when she remembers — well, when I remember". Nobody has reviewed her pain since the dementia advanced; she can’t reliably report it herself.

2–3 hours’ broken sleep, chest "tight" twice last week climbing the stairs (dismissed: "just tired"), no day off in two years, son in Plymouth "has his own troubles", carers refused by Joan early on and never re-offered.

Only if his exhaustion is heard without judgement: "Last Tuesday, at the door, I grabbed her arm. Hard. Properly hard — there’s a mark, doctor. I frightened myself. My Joan, sixty years, and I left a mark on her. That’s really why I’m ringing. I don’t trust myself at 3am any more."
Officially: a sleeping tablet for Joan. Actually: to confess Tuesday, to be told whether he’s become dangerous, and for someone to take the nights off him before something worse happens.

ice.ideas: "A tablet for her" — sedate the problem. He’s heard "they can give them something" at the carers’ coffee morning he went to once.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — Tuesday’s grabbed arm and the mark it left. He believes he is becoming a danger to the woman he’s loved for sixty years, and the sleeping-tablet request is the only way he can open the door to confessing it.
ice.expectations: A prescription tonight. What he needs: the confession received without destroying him, the nights re-engineered (pain, naps, light, routine), real respite, and his own chest pain taken seriously.

cues: "I’m eighty-three. I can’t keep doing nights." — the carer is the second patient; this sentence is HIS presenting complaint.
"Chest’s been tight on the stairs — just tired" — dropped in passing; an 83-year-old with new exertional chest tightness is its own urgent consultation.
The long pause before "I’ll not waste your time" cracks — and later: "That’s really why I’m ringing." The tablet was never the agenda.

checkpoints.text: Hunts the drivers of the 2am waking instead of reaching for sedation: untreated OA pain (grimacing, rubbing, PRN paracetamol she can’t request), two daytime naps, afternoon tea (caffeine), streetlit room, evening TV light, reduced daytime activity — each named as fixable

Declines the sleeping tablet with the honest reason: Z-drugs/benzodiazepines in dementia = falls, fractures, worse confusion, faster decline; antipsychotics carry stroke and death warnings and are reserved for severe distress/risk after specialist input — "the tablet that makes tonight quieter makes every week after worse"

Treats the treatable TODAY: pain she cannot report assessed with a structured observational tool (NICE NG97) and treated on a schedule, not PRN — for knee OA NICE NG226 favours topical NSAIDs and exercise and advises against routine paracetamol, so a scheduled topical NSAID with any oral analgesic as a short, reviewed trial; sleep-environment prescription (blackout, nap cap, caffeine cut-off, morning daylight walk); donepezil timing checked (the SPC advises bedtime dosing, but it can cause insomnia and abnormal dreams — moving it to the morning is an off-label timing change, said as such)

Takes Frank’s chest pain seriously as its own presentation: new exertional tightness at 83 = urgent assessment for HIM this week, framed as non-negotiable — "Joan’s care plan collapses without you, and that’s the least important reason"

Receives the Tuesday confession without flinching or minimising: names it as a system failure landing on one exhausted man, not a monster emerging — "the danger isn’t you, Frank; it’s 3am alone, two years without a night off"

Is honest about what the mark means procedurally — gently: it gets documented, Joan gets seen (tomorrow’s visit), and the help that arrives is support, not accusation; secrecy is what makes 3am dangerous, and he’s just ended it

Re-opens the refused-carers question at the right level: Joan refused strangers three years ago; the offer has never been remade — night-sitting service, day centre two days a week, Admiral Nurse, carer’s assessment, respite — started this week, not "looked into"

Safety-nets both patients: Joan — tomorrow’s review visit (knees, mark, medication, weight); Frank — chest pain worse/at rest/with sweating = 999 tonight, GP appointment booked for HIM this week; crisis numbers (Admiral Nurse/dementia support line) given; the GP’s follow-up call dated — "you don’t carry another Tuesday alone"

worked.txt: "Frank, I’m going to be straight, because you deserve straight: the sleeping tablets that exist make dementia worse — more falls, more confusion, faster decline. They’d buy you a quieter Tuesday and cost Joan the rest of the year. But I am NOT leaving you with nothing — there’s a list of things driving these nights, and most of them we can fix this week."

"Start with the thing nobody’s treating: her knees. She grimaces standing and rubs them at night — Joan can’t tell you it hurts any more, so the pain wakes her instead, at 2am, dressed for 1987. An anti-inflammatory gel rubbed into both knees, morning and bedtime, every day — not when she asks, because she can’t ask — plus gentle movement in the day. If that isn’t enough, we try a regular painkiller for a couple of weeks and see whether the nights change. Pain relief is the commonest sleeping tablet nobody prescribes."

"Then the engineering: the two naps go down to one short one before lunch; tea becomes decaf after two; blackout lining behind those thin curtains; a walk in morning daylight, even ten minutes — daylight is the dial that sets her clock. And her donepezil: it’s normally taken at bedtime, but it can stir dreams and waking — I’d like to try it in the morning instead, which is a small change from how it’s licensed, and see if the nights settle. None of this is dramatic. Together they’re stronger than any tablet I could give her."

"Now the thing you actually rang about. … Frank, listen to me carefully. A man who grabs an arm at 3am after two years of no sleep and no help is not a dangerous man — he’s an abandoned one. The mark on Joan’s arm is the system’s mark, and it landed through your hand because you were the only one there. You frightened yourself because you’re a good man. Dangerous men don’t ring their doctor about it."

"Here’s what happens now, and I want you to hear it as help, not trouble: I write down what you’ve told me, I come and see Joan tomorrow — knees, the arm, the lot — and the support that should’ve been there two years ago starts this week: a night-sitter so you SLEEP, a day centre so you breathe, a nurse whose whole job is families like yours. Telling me was the bravest thing you’ve done in this whole illness. Secrecy was the dangerous part — and you’ve just ended it."

"One more thing, and I’m not letting it go: tight chest on the stairs, twice, at eighty-three — that’s not ‘just tired’, that’s a heart asking for attention. You’re booked in this week, no arguments. And if it comes on at rest, or with sweating, or won’t ease — that’s 999 tonight, and you tell them about Joan and they’ll sort her too. You’ve kept Joan alive for three years, Frank. This week, somebody looks after you."

f.learning: Night-time disturbance in dementia is a cause-hunt, not a prescription: untreated pain (assess with an observational tool and treat on a schedule — topical NSAIDs first for knee OA per NICE NG226; she cannot request PRN), daytime napping, caffeine, light, inactivity, and cholinesterase-inhibitor timing (bedtime per the SPC; a morning move is off-label) all drive 2am waking — while Z-drugs worsen falls and confusion, and antipsychotics carry stroke/death warnings reserved for severe risk after specialist input. The carer is the second patient: new exertional chest pain at 83 is its own urgent presentation. The hidden agenda is the confession — a grabbed arm and a mark — received without panic as carer breakdown, documented honestly, answered with same-week respite and review rather than accusation. Secrecy, not Frank, was the danger.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG97 — Dementia: assessment, management and support
knowledge.summary: Night waking in dementia is a search for causes, not a prescription. Hunt the drivers (pain, naps, caffeine, light, inactivity, medication timing), avoid hypnotics and antipsychotics, and treat the carer as the second patient.

points.t: Untreated pain she cannot report, two daytime naps, afternoon tea, a streetlit room, evening TV, less daytime activity, and a cholinesterase inhibitor that can cause insomnia and abnormal dreams. Rule out delirium if the change is sudden (infection, constipation, urinary retention, new drugs).

points.h: Pain in someone who can’t say it hurts
points.t: NICE NG97: assess pain with a structured observational tool when the person cannot self-report, and consider pain as a cause of distress. For knee OA, NICE NG226 favours topical NSAIDs and exercise; a regular scheduled analgesic trial, reviewed, suits someone who cannot ask for PRN doses.

NICE NG97 advises a personalised, multicomponent sleep plan: sleep-hygiene education, daylight exposure, exercise and personalised activities. BNF: donepezil is usually taken at bedtime; if sleep is disturbed, discuss moving it to the morning with the prescriber (an off-label timing change).

Benzodiazepines and Z-drugs in older people with dementia bring falls, fractures and worse confusion. Antipsychotics increase stroke risk and mortality in dementia (BNF). Risperidone is licensed only short-term, up to 6 weeks, for persistent aggression in moderate to severe Alzheimer’s. If ever used, NICE NG97 asks for review at least every 6 weeks.

A carer-strain incident disclosed by the carer himself. Document it factually, examine Joan, and judge whether it is a single exhaustion-driven event or a pattern. Respond with support straight away: carer’s assessment and respite (Care Act 2014), night-sitting, day centre, Admiral Nurse. Escalate to a Care Act s42 safeguarding referral if there is a pattern, injury beyond what was described, or support is refused.

New exertional chest tightness at 83 needs assessment this week under NICE CG95 (chest pain of recent onset). Tell him to call 999 for pain at rest, pain lasting over 15 minutes, or pain with sweating or breathlessness. NICE NG150 (supporting adult carers): identify carers and look after their own health.

dg.d: Let Frank describe the nights fully; checked Joan’s immediate safety; didn’t argue about the tablet at the start.
Frank’s sleep, no day off in two years, son far away, carers refused and never re-offered, his own health.
Home visit: knees, arm mark, weight, bowels and bladder, delirium screen; structured pain assessment; Frank examined and ECG this week.
Pain, napping, caffeine, light, inactivity, donepezil timing, delirium, disease progression.
Screened for delirium in Joan; identified Frank’s new exertional chest pain and gave 999 triggers.
Night-time disturbance in dementia with treatable drivers, plus severe carer strain with a disclosed incident.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: No hypnotic or antipsychotic; scheduled analgesia; sleep plan; donepezil timing reviewed; respite and carer support this week.
Proportionate safeguarding: documented, Joan examined, support first, escalation criteria clear; Frank’s BP and chest.
Visit tomorrow, Frank seen this week, crisis plan for another bad night, 999 triggers, follow-up call dated.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: “I can’t keep doing nights”, the chest tightness dropped in passing, and the long pause before the confession.
Idea (a tablet will fix it); concern (the grabbed arm, fear he is dangerous); expectation (a prescription tonight).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — Tuesday’s grabbed arm and the mark it left. He believes he is becoming a danger to the woman he’s loved for sixty years, and the sleeping-tablet request is the only way he can open the door to confessing it — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Mr Tully, it’s Dr Hughes. That sounds exhausting. Before anything else: is Joan safe right now, and are you somewhere you can talk?
model.why: Acknowledges him and checks immediate safety on a phone call

model.text: She’s asleep in the chair. Of course she is, in the daytime. I’m in the kitchen.

Right. I heard you: you need something for the nights, and you can’t keep doing them. I want to understand what’s driving the waking, and how you are too, and then we’ll make a plan today. Is that all right?
model.why: Reflects both problems and sets the agenda

model.text: Go on then.
Tell me about her days. When does she sleep, what does she drink, how much does she get about?
She naps eleven till one, then again after tea. I let her; it’s the only peace I get. Tea and biscuits all afternoon. Telly till ten. She walks less since her knees got bad.
Her knees. Does she seem in pain?
model.why: Follows the pain cue in someone who cannot self-report

model.text: She grimaces getting up. Rubs them at night. Paracetamol now and then, when I remember.
And when does she take her donepezil? Anything new, like a temperature, waterworks trouble or constipation?
model.why: Checks medication timing and screens for delirium

model.text: At bedtime. Nothing new like that. It’s been getting worse for six weeks.
And you, Frank? How are you holding up?
model.why: Treats the carer as the second patient

model.text: Two, three hours, in bits. No day off in two years. The lad’s in Plymouth. My chest’s been tight on the stairs a couple of times. Just tired.
I’ll come back to that chest, because it matters. Is there anything else about the nights you haven’t told me yet?
model.why: Flags the chest and leaves room for the hidden agenda

model.text: (long pause) Last Tuesday, at the door, I grabbed her arm. Hard. There’s a mark. Sixty years, and I left a mark on her. I frightened myself. That’s really why I’m ringing.

Thank you for telling me, Frank. That took courage. You’ve had two years without a proper night’s sleep and nobody sharing the nights. That’s the dangerous part, and by ringing me you’ve already started to change it.
model.why: Receives the confession without flinching or minimising

model.text: Am I a danger to her?
Has anything like that happened before, or since?
Never. Not once in sixty years.

I’ll be honest about what happens next, and I want you to hear it as help. I’ll write down what you’ve told me. I’d like to visit tomorrow to see Joan — her knees, her arm, her tablets. And we get you proper help this week. What were you hoping I’d do when you rang?
model.why: Honest about documentation and review; elicits expectations

model.text: A tablet to make her sleep. So I can sleep.

I understand. Straight answer: sleeping tablets in dementia cause falls, broken hips and more confusion, and the stronger calming drugs carry a risk of stroke. They’d make one night quieter and the rest of the year worse. But I’m not leaving you with nothing.
model.why: Declines sedation with the honest reason

model.text: Then what?
Her knees first. Joan can’t tell you it hurts any more, so pain may be what wakes her. Regular painkillers at set times, not only when she seems sore, and I’ll look at her knees tomorrow.
model.why: Scheduled analgesia for pain she cannot report

model.text: Then the day: one short nap before lunch instead of two, decaf after lunchtime, ten minutes outside in the morning light, blackout lining for the curtains. And her donepezil can disturb sleep; I’ll look at moving it to the morning.
model.why: Multicomponent sleep plan and medication timing

model.text: And you need nights off. Joan refused carers three years ago, but nobody’s asked again. Could we start with a carer’s assessment from the council, a night-sitting service, a day centre two days a week, and an Admiral Nurse? I’ll start the referrals today.
model.why: Remakes the refused offer and makes it concrete

model.text: She might go to a day centre if I’m with her the first time.
That’s a good start. Now your chest. Tightness on the stairs at eighty-three isn’t just tiredness. I want you seen this week. I’ll book it before we finish.
model.why: Frank’s exertional chest pain treated as its own urgent problem

model.text: Who’ll watch Joan?

We’ll fit it around the visit, and the carer help is part of the answer. If the chest pain comes on at rest, lasts more than fifteen minutes, or comes with sweating or breathlessness, ring 999 and tell them about Joan.

So: I visit tomorrow; regular painkillers; one nap, decaf, morning light, blackout lining; carer referrals today; you seen this week. If there’s another night when you feel you might lose control, walk away, make sure she’s safe, and ring the dementia support line or 111. Can you tell me back the plan?
You’re coming tomorrow. Tablets regular. One nap. Help for nights. And my chest this week.
Exactly. I’ll ring you on Friday as well. You don’t have to carry another Tuesday on your own.
model.why: Dated follow-up; ends with support, not blame

model.text: Thank you, doctor. I thought you’d think I was a monster.

social.t: An 83-year-old sole carer: broken sleep, no respite for two years, a son far away, and help refused once and never re-offered. His exhaustion is the main risk to both of them.

Attendance Allowance for Joan (not means-tested); council tax reduction for severe mental impairment; blackout lining and door sensors through the council’s occupational therapy or assistive technology service.

legal.t: Frank has a right to a carer’s assessment (s10). The local authority must make enquiries under s42 when an adult with care needs is, or may be, at risk of abuse. Use this if the incident is part of a pattern or support is refused.
Joan probably can’t consent to day care or sharing information herself. Decisions are made in her best interests, involving Frank. Ask whether a health and welfare LPA exists.
Frank’s chest pain is his own consultation: record it in his notes and book him separately. Sharing Joan’s information with her carer is justified in her best interests.

professional.t: GMC Good Medical Practice: protect the vulnerable patient and treat the carer fairly. Documenting and examining are not accusations; say so.
Declining a requested hypnotic is good prescribing, not obstruction. Explain the harms and offer an alternative plan.

community.t: Admiral Nurses (Dementia UK helpline), Alzheimer’s Society, local carers’ centre, day centres and night-sitting services; NICE NG150 on identifying and supporting adult carers.

redFlags: Frank: new exertional chest tightness at 83 — assess this week; 999 for pain at rest, over 15 minutes, or with sweating
Joan: sudden change over days (delirium: infection, retention, constipation, new drugs)
A disclosed injury: examine, document, and establish single event versus pattern
psychosocial: Frank sleeping 2–3 hours in bits; no day off in two years; son in Plymouth
Carers refused three years ago and never re-offered
Joan cannot report pain; less walking; long daytime naps
ice: Idea: “There must be a tablet to make her sleep.”
Concern: he grabbed her arm and left a mark, and fears he is becoming dangerous
Expectation: a prescription tonight; underneath, someone to take the nights off him

playbook.diagnosis: Night-time disturbance in Alzheimer’s disease with treatable drivers (probable untreated OA pain, daytime napping, caffeine, light, donepezil timing), alongside severe carer strain with a single disclosed incident and new exertional chest pain in the carer.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Joan’s body clock has been knocked about. Long naps, tea in the afternoon, a bright room and sore knees she can’t tell you about. Put together, they wake her at two in the morning. And you’re running on empty, which is the most urgent part.”

management.reflectIce: “You rang for a tablet, but what you really needed to tell me was Tuesday. You’ve done the hardest part. Now let’s make sure you’re not on your own at 3am.”
management.psychosocial: Carer’s assessment, night-sitting, day centre and Admiral Nurse referrals started today; proportionate safeguarding (document, examine, support, escalate if a pattern emerges); Frank booked for his own chest pain and BP.
sharedPlan: No hypnotic or antipsychotic; explain why (BNF stroke and mortality warning; falls)
Scheduled analgesia after a structured pain assessment; topical NSAID for knees (NICE NG226); consider moving donepezil to the morning
Sleep plan: one short nap, decaf after lunch, morning daylight, blackout lining, evening wind-down
safetyNet: Home visit tomorrow; Frank seen this week; 999 triggers for chest pain
Crisis plan for another bad night (step away, keep Joan safe, call the helpline or 111); GP call on Friday

pitfalls.intro: This telephone station hides two patients and a confession behind a prescription request. Candidates fail by arguing about the tablet, missing the carer’s chest pain, or mishandling the disclosure in either direction.

items.fail: Prescribing zopiclone, lorazepam or low-dose quetiapine “just for a few nights”.
items.why: Sedatives in dementia cause falls, fractures and worse confusion, and antipsychotics carry stroke and mortality warnings. “Management not in line with UK practice.”
items.fix: Decline with the reason, then offer a real plan: pain, naps, caffeine, light, donepezil timing, respite.

items.fail: Never asking about Joan’s knees or pain.
items.why: Pain in someone who can’t report it is a leading cause of night-time distress. PRN analgesia doesn’t work if she can’t ask for it.
items.fix: “Does she seem sore?” Then scheduled analgesia and a structured pain assessment at the visit.

items.fail: Letting “my chest’s been tight on the stairs” pass as tiredness.
items.why: New exertional chest pain at 83 needs its own urgent assessment. Missing it is a safety failure.
items.fix: Name it, book him this week, and give 999 triggers.

items.fail: Responding to the confession with alarm (“I’ll have to report you”) or with dismissal (“don’t worry about it”).
items.why: The first ends honest disclosure; the second fails Joan. Both lose the Relating domain.
items.fix: Thank him, check single event or pattern, explain honestly that it is documented and Joan is examined, and lead with support.

items.fail: Treating Frank only as a messenger for Joan’s problem.
items.why: “Did not explore the impact on the carer.” His exhaustion is the presenting complaint.
items.fix: “And how are you, Frank?” early on, then a concrete respite plan.

items.fail: “I’ll ask social services to get in touch” as the whole support plan.
items.why: Vague signposting after two years of no help won’t change the next night.
items.fix: Name each service, start the referrals today, and date your own follow-up call.

timeMap.d: Let him get it all out. Check Joan is safe now. Note “I’m eighty-three, I can’t keep doing nights”: that sentence is his own presenting complaint.
Naps, caffeine, light, activity, knees, donepezil timing, delirium screen. Ask how he is. Leave space; the confession arrives if you haven’t judged him.
Receive the grabbed arm calmly. Single event or pattern? Be honest: it gets written down, Joan gets seen, and help arrives.
Decline the tablet with the reason. Pain, naps, decaf, daylight, blackout lining, donepezil timing. Respite, night-sitting, day centre, Admiral Nurse. Frank’s chest this week.
Home visit tomorrow, 999 triggers for Frank, a plan for another bad night, follow-up call dated, teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Prescribes a hypnotic or antipsychotic to end the call, or refuses and offers nothing; never asks about pain, naps or light; misses Frank’s chest pain; never hears the confession, or hears it and turns punitive, or minimises it and does nothing.
wordPics.pass: Declines sedation with a reason, looks for drivers including pain and naps, offers practical sleep measures and carer support, notes Frank’s chest pain and books him in, and responds to the disclosure with documentation and a visit.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: scheduled analgesia framed as “she can’t ask”; donepezil timing reviewed; receives the confession warmly and honestly (single event, document, examine, support first, escalation criteria clear); remakes the carers offer concretely this week; 999 triggers for Frank; the call ends with a dated follow-up and a plan for the next bad night.

avoid.dont: “I can give her something mild to help her settle at night.”
avoid.instead: “Sleeping tablets make dementia worse. Falls, confusion, faster decline. Let’s fix what’s waking her.”
avoid.why: Sedation in dementia causes harm and leaves the real drivers untreated.

avoid.dont: “I’m afraid I have to report this to social services.”
avoid.instead: “I’ll write down what you’ve told me, see Joan tomorrow, and get you proper help this week. Telling me was the right thing.”
avoid.why: Leading with a threat shuts down the disclosure. Proportionate action starts with support, and escalation stays available.

avoid.dont: “Don’t worry, anyone would have done the same.”
avoid.instead: “You were exhausted and alone, and that’s what we change now. I’ll still need to see Joan’s arm.”
avoid.why: Minimising the incident fails the safeguarding duty to Joan.

Her knees. Does she seem in pain?

SCA_MODELS.text: She grimaces getting up. Rubs them at night. Paracetamol now and then, when I remember.
And when does she take her donepezil? Anything new, like a temperature, waterworks trouble or constipation?
SCA_MODELS.why: Checks medication timing and screens for delirium

SCA_MODELS.text: At bedtime. Nothing new like that. It’s been getting worse for six weeks.
And you, Frank? How are you holding up?
SCA_MODELS.why: Treats the carer as the second patient

SCA_MODELS.text: Two, three hours, in bits. No day off in two years. The lad’s in Plymouth. My chest’s been tight on the stairs a couple of times. Just tired.
I’ll come back to that chest, because it matters. Is there anything else about the nights you haven’t told me yet?
SCA_MODELS.why: Flags the chest and leaves room for the hidden agenda

SCA_MODELS.text: (long pause) Last Tuesday, at the door, I grabbed her arm. Hard. There’s a mark. Sixty years, and I left a mark on her. I frightened myself. That’s really why I’m ringing.

Thank you for telling me, Frank. That took courage. You’ve had two years without a proper night’s sleep and nobody sharing the nights. That’s the dangerous part, and by ringing me you’ve already started to change it.
SCA_MODELS.why: Receives the confession without flinching or minimising

SCA_MODELS.text: Am I a danger to her?
Has anything like that happened before, or since?
Never. Not once in sixty years.

I’ll be honest about what happens next, and I want you to hear it as help. I’ll write down what you’ve told me. I’d like to visit tomorrow to see Joan — her knees, her arm, her tablets. And we get you proper help this week. What were you hoping I’d do when you rang?
SCA_MODELS.why: Honest about documentation and review; elicits expectations

SCA_MODELS.text: A tablet to make her sleep. So I can sleep.

I understand. Straight answer: sleeping tablets in dementia cause falls, broken hips and more confusion, and the stronger calming drugs carry a risk of stroke. They’d make one night quieter and the rest of the year worse. But I’m not leaving you with nothing.
SCA_MODELS.why: Declines sedation with the honest reason

SCA_MODELS.text: Then what?
Her knees first. Joan can’t tell you it hurts any more, so pain may be what wakes her. Regular painkillers at set times, not only when she seems sore, and I’ll look at her knees tomorrow.
SCA_MODELS.why: Scheduled analgesia for pain she cannot report

SCA_MODELS.text: Then the day: one short nap before lunch instead of two, decaf after lunchtime, ten minutes outside in the morning light, blackout lining for the curtains. And her donepezil can disturb sleep; I’ll look at moving it to the morning.
SCA_MODELS.why: Multicomponent sleep plan and medication timing

SCA_MODELS.text: And you need nights off. Joan refused carers three years ago, but nobody’s asked again. Could we start with a carer’s assessment from the council, a night-sitting service, a day centre two days a week, and an Admiral Nurse? I’ll start the referrals today.
SCA_MODELS.why: Remakes the refused offer and makes it concrete

SCA_MODELS.text: She might go to a day centre if I’m with her the first time.
That’s a good start. Now your chest. Tightness on the stairs at eighty-three isn’t just tiredness. I want you seen this week. I’ll book it before we finish.
SCA_MODELS.why: Frank’s exertional chest pain treated as its own urgent problem

SCA_MODELS.text: Who’ll watch Joan?

We’ll fit it around the visit, and the carer help is part of the answer. If the chest pain comes on at rest, lasts more than fifteen minutes, or comes with sweating or breathlessness, ring 999 and tell them about Joan.

So: I visit tomorrow; regular painkillers; one nap, decaf, morning light, blackout lining; carer referrals today; you seen this week. If there’s another night when you feel you might lose control, walk away, make sure she’s safe, and ring the dementia support line or 111. Can you tell me back the plan?
You’re coming tomorrow. Tablets regular. One nap. Help for nights. And my chest this week.
Exactly. I’ll ring you on Friday as well. You don’t have to carry another Tuesday on your own.
SCA_MODELS.why: Dated follow-up; ends with support, not blame

SCA_MODELS.text: Thank you, doctor. I thought you’d think I was a monster.

SCA_STEM.name: Joan Tully
SCA_STEM.recent: Last review: “grimaces on standing”. Lives at home with her husband Frank, 83, her sole carer. Frank is also registered here: BP raised at last check; one attendance in 5 years.
SCA_STEM.reason: Husband Frank is calling about six weeks of night-time waking. He is asking for “something to make her sleep”.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG97 — Dementia: assessment, management and support
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Night waking in dementia is a search for causes, not a prescription. Hunt the drivers (pain, naps, caffeine, light, inactivity, medication timing), avoid hypnotics and antipsychotics, and treat the carer as the second patient.

points.t: Untreated pain she cannot report, two daytime naps, afternoon tea, a streetlit room, evening TV, less daytime activity, and a cholinesterase inhibitor that can cause insomnia and abnormal dreams. Rule out delirium if the change is sudden (infection, constipation, urinary retention, new drugs).

points.h: Pain in someone who can’t say it hurts
points.t: NICE NG97: assess pain with a structured observational tool when the person cannot self-report, and consider pain as a cause of distress. For knee OA, NICE NG226 favours topical NSAIDs and exercise; a regular scheduled analgesic trial, reviewed, suits someone who cannot ask for PRN doses.

NICE NG97 advises a personalised, multicomponent sleep plan: sleep-hygiene education, daylight exposure, exercise and personalised activities. BNF: donepezil is usually taken at bedtime; if sleep is disturbed, discuss moving it to the morning with the prescriber (an off-label timing change).

Benzodiazepines and Z-drugs in older people with dementia bring falls, fractures and worse confusion. Antipsychotics increase stroke risk and mortality in dementia (BNF). Risperidone is licensed only short-term, up to 6 weeks, for persistent aggression in moderate to severe Alzheimer’s. If ever used, NICE NG97 asks for review at least every 6 weeks.

A carer-strain incident disclosed by the carer himself. Document it factually, examine Joan, and judge whether it is a single exhaustion-driven event or a pattern. Respond with support straight away: carer’s assessment and respite (Care Act 2014), night-sitting, day centre, Admiral Nurse. Escalate to a Care Act s42 safeguarding referral if there is a pattern, injury beyond what was described, or support is refused.

New exertional chest tightness at 83 needs assessment this week under NICE CG95 (chest pain of recent onset). Tell him to call 999 for pain at rest, pain lasting over 15 minutes, or pain with sweating or breathlessness. NICE NG150 (supporting adult carers): identify carers and look after their own health.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Let Frank describe the nights fully; checked Joan’s immediate safety; didn’t argue about the tablet at the start.
Frank’s sleep, no day off in two years, son far away, carers refused and never re-offered, his own health.
“I can’t keep doing nights”, the chest tightness dropped in passing, and the long pause before the confession.
Idea (a tablet will fix it); concern (the grabbed arm, fear he is dangerous); expectation (a prescription tonight).
Home visit: knees, arm mark, weight, bowels and bladder, delirium screen; structured pain assessment; Frank examined and ECG this week.
Pain, napping, caffeine, light, inactivity, donepezil timing, delirium, disease progression.
Screened for delirium in Joan; identified Frank’s new exertional chest pain and gave 999 triggers.
Night-time disturbance in dementia with treatable drivers, plus severe carer strain with a disclosed incident.
No hypnotic or antipsychotic; scheduled analgesia; sleep plan; donepezil timing reviewed; respite and carer support this week.
Proportionate safeguarding: documented, Joan examined, support first, escalation criteria clear; Frank’s BP and chest.
Visit tomorrow, Frank seen this week, crisis plan for another bad night, 999 triggers, follow-up call dated.

social.t: An 83-year-old sole carer: broken sleep, no respite for two years, a son far away, and help refused once and never re-offered. His exhaustion is the main risk to both of them.

Attendance Allowance for Joan (not means-tested); council tax reduction for severe mental impairment; blackout lining and door sensors through the council’s occupational therapy or assistive technology service.

legal.t: Frank has a right to a carer’s assessment (s10). The local authority must make enquiries under s42 when an adult with care needs is, or may be, at risk of abuse. Use this if the incident is part of a pattern or support is refused.
Joan probably can’t consent to day care or sharing information herself. Decisions are made in her best interests, involving Frank. Ask whether a health and welfare LPA exists.
Frank’s chest pain is his own consultation: record it in his notes and book him separately. Sharing Joan’s information with her carer is justified in her best interests.

professional.t: GMC Good Medical Practice: protect the vulnerable patient and treat the carer fairly. Documenting and examining are not accusations; say so.
Declining a requested hypnotic is good prescribing, not obstruction. Explain the harms and offer an alternative plan.

community.t: Admiral Nurses (Dementia UK helpline), Alzheimer’s Society, local carers’ centre, day centres and night-sitting services; NICE NG150 on identifying and supporting adult carers.

redFlags: Frank: new exertional chest tightness at 83 — assess this week; 999 for pain at rest, over 15 minutes, or with sweating
Joan: sudden change over days (delirium: infection, retention, constipation, new drugs)
A disclosed injury: examine, document, and establish single event versus pattern
psychosocial: Frank sleeping 2–3 hours in bits; no day off in two years; son in Plymouth
Carers refused three years ago and never re-offered
Joan cannot report pain; less walking; long daytime naps
ice: Idea: “There must be a tablet to make her sleep.”
Concern: he grabbed her arm and left a mark, and fears he is becoming dangerous
Expectation: a prescription tonight; underneath, someone to take the nights off him

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Night-time disturbance in Alzheimer’s disease with treatable drivers (probable untreated OA pain, daytime napping, caffeine, light, donepezil timing), alongside severe carer strain with a single disclosed incident and new exertional chest pain in the carer.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Joan’s body clock has been knocked about. Long naps, tea in the afternoon, a bright room and sore knees she can’t tell you about. Put together, they wake her at two in the morning. And you’re running on empty, which is the most urgent part.”

management.reflectIce: “You rang for a tablet, but what you really needed to tell me was Tuesday. You’ve done the hardest part. Now let’s make sure you’re not on your own at 3am.”
management.psychosocial: Carer’s assessment, night-sitting, day centre and Admiral Nurse referrals started today; proportionate safeguarding (document, examine, support, escalate if a pattern emerges); Frank booked for his own chest pain and BP.
sharedPlan: No hypnotic or antipsychotic; explain why (BNF stroke and mortality warning; falls)
Scheduled analgesia after a structured pain assessment; topical NSAID for knees (NICE NG226); consider moving donepezil to the morning
Sleep plan: one short nap, decaf after lunch, morning daylight, blackout lining, evening wind-down
safetyNet: Home visit tomorrow; Frank seen this week; 999 triggers for chest pain
Crisis plan for another bad night (step away, keep Joan safe, call the helpline or 111); GP call on Friday

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This telephone station hides two patients and a confession behind a prescription request. Candidates fail by arguing about the tablet, missing the carer’s chest pain, or mishandling the disclosure in either direction.

items.fail: Prescribing zopiclone, lorazepam or low-dose quetiapine “just for a few nights”.
items.why: Sedatives in dementia cause falls, fractures and worse confusion, and antipsychotics carry stroke and mortality warnings. “Management not in line with UK practice.”
items.fix: Decline with the reason, then offer a real plan: pain, naps, caffeine, light, donepezil timing, respite.

items.fail: Never asking about Joan’s knees or pain.
items.why: Pain in someone who can’t report it is a leading cause of night-time distress. PRN analgesia doesn’t work if she can’t ask for it.
items.fix: “Does she seem sore?” Then scheduled analgesia and a structured pain assessment at the visit.

items.fail: Letting “my chest’s been tight on the stairs” pass as tiredness.
items.why: New exertional chest pain at 83 needs its own urgent assessment. Missing it is a safety failure.
items.fix: Name it, book him this week, and give 999 triggers.

items.fail: Responding to the confession with alarm (“I’ll have to report you”) or with dismissal (“don’t worry about it”).
items.why: The first ends honest disclosure; the second fails Joan. Both lose the Relating domain.
items.fix: Thank him, check single event or pattern, explain honestly that it is documented and Joan is examined, and lead with support.

items.fail: Treating Frank only as a messenger for Joan’s problem.
items.why: “Did not explore the impact on the carer.” His exhaustion is the presenting complaint.
items.fix: “And how are you, Frank?” early on, then a concrete respite plan.

items.fail: “I’ll ask social services to get in touch” as the whole support plan.
items.why: Vague signposting after two years of no help won’t change the next night.
items.fix: Name each service, start the referrals today, and date your own follow-up call.
